title: Verdant Labs Dedicated Node Sizing + Hybrid Burst Workshop
next_steps: Maya to share tailored pricing + prewarm/cost spreadsheet by 2026-08-21
Luis to run a short latency/throughput micro-benchmark (50k tokens/day profile) and share results by 2026-08-24
Verdant to provide recent traffic histogram (1 week) and typical prompt length by 2026-08-22
Schedule follow-up 30-min architecture deep dive the week of 2026-08-31
action_items: Maya Chen - Send reserved vs hosted cost model + spreadsheet - 2026-08-21
Luis Ortega - Run benchmark (gpt-like 2k seq) and attach logs - 2026-08-24
Daniel Park - Share 7-day qps/latency histogram and top 10 endpoints - 2026-08-22
Nina Rao - Confirm regulatory boundary (EU data residency?) and KMS requirements - 2026-08-25
transcript: 00:00:03 - Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining. i'm maya, account exec on the redwood side. luis is here from solutions engineering. how's everyone doing?
00:00:10 - Daniel Park: good, thanks. daniel here. we wanted to run through dedicated sizing and the hybrid burst idea — basically how we keep costs predictable but handle spikes from our mobile app.
00:00:21 - Nina Rao: hi all, nina. a bit of context — we run inference for summarization + rerank, average 1.8k tokens per session but tail goes up to 6k on long docs.
00:00:32 - Marcus Li: marcus here, i'm mostly focused on ops: isolation, preemption, and how failover works if one pool is saturated.

00:00:40 - Luis Ortega: great, thanks. quick agenda: confirm traffic/profile, sizing options (reserved pools, hot-pools, hybrid hosted fallback), prewarm & KV caching, and security/VPC questions. sound good?
00:00:50 - Daniel Park: yep, let's go.
00:02:05 - Luis Ortega: can i ask about current qps and token mix? you mentioned average tokens but what about RPS distribution?

00:02:14 - Nina Rao: so baseline is around 12 rps, spikes up to 120 rps during release windows. most calls are short — 75% under 2k tokens, 10% between 2k-4k, 5% above that, and the rest are rare long-running transcripts.

00:02:34 - Maya Chen: okay that profile maps to a mix of sustained capacity plus burst. reserved nodes for steady-state, and a burst strategy for those 10x spikes. do you have a preferred SLA/latency goal?
00:02:45 - Daniel Park: p95 latency ideally under 300ms for generation on our primary endpoints. willingness to accept slightly higher tail during rare peaks but prefer predictable billing.

00:02:56 - Marcus Li: also we need tenant isolation — we can't have other teams noisy-neighboring our models. some workloads are regulated so we need per-customer isolation at node or at least namespace level.

00:03:12 - Luis Ortega: understood. isolation is a common ask. in Dedicated we can map pools per-tenancy or per-workload. options are: fully segregated reserved nodes, soft multi-tenant with cgroup limits, or dedicate hot-pools for regulated traffic. tradeoffs are cost vs utilization.
00:04:01 - Nina Rao: can you explain hot-pool vs warm-pool? i've seen different terms in docs.

00:04:05 - Luis Ortega: yeah, sorry for jargon. hot-pool = prewarmed GPUs with model loaded and kv cache warm so first token latency is low. warm-pool = instances are ready but model load happens on request which adds startup penalty. hot-pool consumes more hours but reduces tail latency. there's also continuous KV caching that helps if prompts share prefixes.

00:04:28 - Daniel Park: for us, p95 is important for UX. if hot-pool reduces p95 from 600ms to 240ms, probably worth it for core endpoints. but cost is concern — what savings do you see vs pure hosted?

00:04:40 - Maya Chen: typically reserved dedicated nodes give unit-cost savings vs hosted, because you commit capacity. plus you get isolation. we ran a model for a customer where dedicated reduced per-token cost by ~30% vs hosted at similar latency when fully utilized. that said, burst to hosted is common to avoid overprovisioning.
00:04:55 - Marcus Li: how does fallback work if our reserved pool fills? does it automatically route to hosted variant? how do you handle auth and network when some requests go to hosted?

00:05:06 - Luis Ortega: we support smart routing policies: priority to dedicated pool, then region-matched hosted, then lower-cost quantized variant. For VPC/private deployments we do a secure peered egress path — we can route traffic to hosted only if you allow an exit point. if that's not acceptable, we can expand dedicated or enable burst nodes in your private infra (on-prem) depending on contract.

00:05:30 - Nina Rao: ok, that matters — for EU-regulated PII we can't send traffic outside our VPC. we need a model for dedicated-only burst within our VPC or adding extra reserved nodes during expected peaks.

00:05:42 - Maya Chen: got it. so two paths: 1) Dedicated-only with larger reserved + predictive autoscale buffer, or 2) Hybrid where non-PII routes can burst to hosted. we'll map endpoints and policies.
00:07:00 - Daniel Park: can you walk through an example sizing calc? say baseline 12 rps with 1.8k tokens avg, spike 120 rps for 15 minutes — how many GPUs?

00:07:12 - Luis Ortega: sure. rough numbers: assume model throughput ~25 tokens/sec per GPU for that sequence length (very model-dependent). 1.8k tokens -> ~72s per request if single-threaded, but with batching continuous runtime increases throughput. For 12 rps sustained you need throughput of ~21600 tokens/sec, wait that math seems off, sorry. let me reframe: tokens/sec demand = rps * avg_tokens. so baseline 12 * 1800 = 21.6k tokens/sec. if a GPU yields 25 tokens/sec, you'd need ~864 GPUs — that's obviously inconsistent and i misspoke. the actual deployed numbers use batching and more like 500-2k tokens/sec per GPU for optimized runtimes.
00:07:55 - Daniel Park: okay, there was a miscalc, but point is these numbers swing a lot depending on model, batching, and kernel optimizations.

00:08:03 - Luis Ortega: right — sorry about the confusion. maybe better to say: with our optimized runtime and batching, a single A100-style node can handle hundreds of concurrent short requests at 2k tokens with good batching, but long sequences reduce effective throughput. we'll run a bench with your payload to get precise numbers.

00:08:20 - Maya Chen: action item: luis will run a targeted micro-benchmark using Verdant sample prompts to produce GPUs-needed at p95 target. we'll include both warm and hot-pool configs. that was one of the next steps.
00:09:15 - Nina Rao: how does quantization affect latency/quality? we have some non-critical internal endpoints where slight quality drop is fine for big savings.

00:09:23 - Luis Ortega: quantization profiles are a levers: int8/4 reduce memory footprint and increase effective throughput but can add small quality regressions. Redwood Optimize can suggest quantization per endpoint; you can run an eval suite to detect regressions. for internal endpoints quantization + hosted burst often gets good unit cost improvements.
00:10:02 - Daniel Park: we also have a regulatory question. we need KMS-managed keys and audit logs for inference payloads — can you confirm options?

00:10:10 - Maya Chen: Dedicated and Private both integrate with customer KMS/HSM. audit logs can be exported to your SIEM, and we have configurable retention. we'll attach SOC2 cert and our security deck.
00:10:25 - Marcus Li: what's the network topology for Private? we want no egress to public internet for certain models.

00:10:30 - Luis Ortega: Private deployment runs in customer VPC or on-prem. control plane connectivity can be tunneled; data plane stays in your network. For zero-egress we offer an air-gapped on-prem installer but that increases onboarding time and constraints on supported GPUs.
00:11:00 - Nina Rao: onboarding time — what's realistic for dedicated vs private?
00:11:05 - Maya Chen: Dedicated (hosted Redwood-managed reserved pool) ~4-6 weeks for standard contracts. Private (VPC-managed) ~6-10 weeks depending on networking and KMS. on-prem ~8-14 weeks.
00:11:20 - Daniel Park: that's helpful. pricing thoughts? if we reserved N nodes month-to-month vs 12-month commit?

00:11:27 - Maya Chen: month-to-month is higher unit price but flexible. annual commits give significant discounts. we'll show a comparison in the spreadsheet for typical N sizes and utilization rates. Also consider burst credit allocation — you pay lower for reserved and pay per-use for burst.
00:12:55 - Marcus Li: curious about failure modes: if a dedicated node goes down during a spike and we're relying on it, what's the SLA and failover pattern?

00:13:03 - Luis Ortega: we have health-checks and automatic routing off failed nodes. for critical endpoints we recommend cross-pool replication + canary fallback to hosted or another region. SLA for Dedicated has uptime SLOs; full enterprise SLAs available under contract.
00:13:22 - Nina Rao: do you support canary/rollouts for model versions in Dedicated? we can't afford bad regression pushing to prod.
00:13:28 - Luis Ortega: yes, Redwood Console supports canaries, A/B, and automatic rollback based on quality metrics or error rates. you can pin routes to model versions and control percentages.
00:14:45 - Daniel Park: operationally, who handles OS/driver updates on dedicated? we need stability — no surprise reboots during business hours.

00:14:53 - Maya Chen: for Redwood-managed dedicated, we schedule maintenance windows, and coordinate with you'll. for VPC/Private you control host-level upgrades, but we provide guidance and an ops playbook.
00:15:30 - Marcus Li: ok, security follow-up: SSO/SAML + RBAC enforcement across teams?
00:15:35 - Luis Ortega: supported — SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning, RBAC policies with route-level controls. we can also integrate with your IAM for fine-grained access.
00:17:00 - Nina Rao: question about metrics: can we get token-level cost attribution per route?
00:17:05 - Maya Chen: yes, Console gives token-level cost and latency breakdown per route and model. that helps identify hotspots and decide which endpoints to quantize or move to hot-pools.
00:18:12 - Daniel Park: thinking about burst sizing, we don't want to overcommit. can you do predictive autoscaling that uses traffic history?

00:18:20 - Luis Ortega: Redwood has workload-aware autoscaling plus predictive suggestions in Redwood Optimize. we can set min reserved capacity and allow burst buffer that prewarms nodes based on predicted window. you can also set hard-fallbacks to prevent runaway spend.

00:19:10 - Maya Chen: real customer story — we had a fintech customer who used a mix of reserved + hosted burst; they set a 20% prewarm buffer and avoided 80% of p95 spikes while keeping committed spend 40% lower than naive overprovisioning. it's a tuning exercise with profiling.
00:20:45 - Daniel Park: great. for the benchmark you mentioned, what artifacts do you need from us?

00:20:50 - Luis Ortega: we'll need a small sample set of typical prompts (5-10 anonymized), desired p95 target, and a representative concurrency pattern (rps distribution). also indicate which endpoints are allowed to burst to hosted vs must stay in-vpc.
00:21:10 - Nina Rao: we'll anonymize and share. also question: do you support model quantization in Private?
00:21:16 - Luis Ortega: yes, quantization profiles and kernel optimizations are supported in Private as well; some quant paths depend on hardware and driver support, but we'll advise per deployment.
00:21:45 - Marcus Li: what about billing granularity for reserved nodes? hourly? monthly?
00:21:50 - Maya Chen: billing options: hourly with minimum commitment, monthly, or annual with discounts. we'll model both in the spreadsheet.
00:23:00 - Daniel Park: any pitfalls we should be aware of when moving from hosted PoC to dedicated?

00:23:06 - Luis Ortega: common ones: underestimating tail sequences (long transcripts), missing prefix-sharing opportunities (no KV cache), and not segmenting endpoints by criticality. we help via evals and prompt set-based regression tests.
00:24:22 - Nina Rao: are there examples of reserved pool sizing for customers with similar profiles (mobile app bursts)?
00:24:28 - Maya Chen: yes — we'll include a sanitized case study in the attachments. i'll drop a link to the sizing workbook. [link: deck and sizing spreadsheet]
00:24:40 - Daniel Park: great. can you also include the private deployment network checklist?
00:24:45 - Maya Chen: yes, network checklist + security deck will be included.

00:26:00 - Luis Ortega: quick note on KV caching: if many requests share prefixes (like system prompts + few user tokens), prefix cache can dramatically reduce token work. it requires model-compatible cache (some models don't benefit). we'll test in the bench.
00:27:30 - Marcus Li: interesting. for our scheduled nightly batch jobs that produce long transcripts, would we route those to separate lower-priority reserved nodes?
00:27:37 - Luis Ortega: that's recommended: isolate long-running batches to separate pool so they don't affect interactive endpoints. this is a tenancy/route-level policy.
00:29:05 - Daniel Park: let's talk about prewarm cost tradeoffs — what's the recommendation for a company of our size?

00:29:12 - Maya Chen: depends on SLO vs spend tradeoff. one pattern: keep reserved capacity for 80-90% baseline, maintain a small hot-pool sized for typical short spikes, and rely on burst to hosted or scheduled reserve increases for known large events. the spreadsheet will show cost curves for utilization bands.
00:31:00 - Nina Rao: does Redwood provide alerts when our pool is near capacity?
00:31:05 - Luis Ortega: yes Console has alerts for utilization thresholds, queued requests, and p95 regressions. you can hook to PagerDuty or Slack.
00:33:20 - Daniel Park: how does rate limiting interplay with reserved pools? we have upstream rate limiting already but want guardrails in case of bad deploys.
00:33:26 - Luis Ortega: we expose rate limits per route and token quotas. you can set per-route hard caps to prevent runaway spend and soft caps that trigger autoscaling/prewarm.
00:35:00 - Maya Chen: quick commercial note — we can include burst credits in the reserved deal to cover expected spikes for the first quarter, eases transition risk.
00:35:10 - Daniel Park: that helps. any other questions from your side?
00:35:24 - Marcus Li: i'd like a summary of maintenance windows and how we coordinate major driver/kernel updates — we want a runbook.
00:35:32 - Luis Ortega: we'll attach the ops runbook and propose a quarterly maintenance cadence with emergency patching options.
00:36:50 - Nina Rao: on the topic of data retention, how long are logs stored by default? can we configure shorter retention for PII endpoints?
00:36:58 - Maya Chen: default retention is 90 days for logs but customizable per account. for PII we can set stricter retention or disable payload logging and only keep telemetry.
00:38:10 - Daniel Park: can we get a cost sensitivity analysis: if our spikes double in frequency, what's the delta vs scaling reserved vs relying on hosted burst?
00:38:18 - Maya Chen: yes we'll model scenarios in the spreadsheet: utilization bands, spike frequency, and show mixed strategy costs. that's part of next steps.

00:40:00 - Luis Ortega: one technical thing to note: if you plan to use multiple model variants (higher capacity vs cheaper quantized), we recommend route-level model mapping and fallback chains so if high-quality model is saturated it falls back to quantized variant rather than failing.
00:41:12 - Daniel Park: how do we test regression when fallback occurs? can't have silent quality drops.
00:41:20 - Luis Ortega: Redwood Optimize can run end-to-end evals on canary traffic; you can set rollback triggers based on BLEU/ROUGE or custom metrics. we'll show sample alert config.

00:43:05 - Maya Chen: quick recap before we close: 1) luis benchmark using anonymized prompts, 2) maya sends pricing + prewarm spreadsheet + security deck, 3) verdant shares traffic histograms and allowed-burst endpoints, 4) schedule follow-up deep dive. everyone okay with that?
00:43:23 - Daniel Park: yep, sounds right.
00:43:28 - Nina Rao: yes, thanks — we'll get the artifacts over this week.
00:43:35 - Marcus Li: one last ops Q — during major region outage do you support cross-region failover for Dedicated?

00:43:40 - Luis Ortega: yes, we can pre-provision a cold-warm failover region and route traffic; it adds cost but ensures availability. we'll include a cross-region plan for high-availability customer playbooks.
00:44:50 - Maya Chen: thanks everyone. i'll drop links in the calendar invite and follow-up email. expect the spreadsheet by friday.
00:44:56 - Daniel Park: thanks maya, luis. good session.
00:45:02 - Nina Rao: thanks all.
00:45:06 - End of recording
